transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. What brings you here today?

Well, hi, yes, thank you for seeing me. Um, it’s kind of a long story, but I guess the short version—well, what finally pushed me to actually make the appointment and come in today—is this thing I keep doing at work, and, well, in my personal life too, honestly. I'm a software developer, right? So we have these meetings, sprint planning mostly, which, if you know anything about Agile, can be incredibly tedious, but they are important. You really have to be there and be present. But I just... I keep getting up. 

It’s like I’m sitting there, and I know, I absolutely know I should stay put, but suddenly I’ll just feel this overwhelming urge that I need a glass of water right that very second, or I’ll suddenly decide I need to go check something in the other room, or look out the window, or see if the mail came, even though it’s 10 AM and the mail never comes before three. And it’s not just work! My husband and I are trying to refinance our house, and we’ll be on these really important mortgage calls with the bank, going over interest rates and escrow and all these details you really can't miss, and I'll still find myself wandering off to the kitchen. My husband will be looking at me like, "What are you doing, get back here," and I just... I can't seem to just stay in my chair when I'm supposed to. It’s starting to get really embarrassing, to be honest, and I just felt like I needed to talk to someone about why I can't just sit through a normal meeting like everyone else.

Has this pattern of getting up or feeling the urge to leave the moment you're supposed to be focused happened in other parts of your life too, like maybe school, social events, or even watching a movie?

Oh, school. Wow, yes. Actually, now that you mention it, it goes way, way back. I mean, all the way back to elementary school. I remember it so vividly. In third grade—Mrs. Gable's class, she had this really brightly decorated room with all these little reading nooks—and she was constantly, and I mean *constantly*, having to remind me to stay in my seat. It was basically a daily occurrence. She actually ended up moving my desk right next to hers at the very front of the room because I was always just popping up out of my chair for no real reason. 

I’d go sharpen my pencil when she was right in the middle of a math lesson, or I'd wander over to look at the class pet, which was a hamster, I think. And it wasn't just the getting up, either. I was always blurting out answers before she even finished asking the question, or talking before I was called on, which I know frustrated her to no end because she had a very strict hand-raising rule. 

And the funny thing is, I actually understood the work! I was a smart kid, I really was, but I would just rush through my assignments at lightning speed so I could be done. Even when I knew exactly how to do the worksheet, I'd just speed through it because I couldn't stand just sitting there working on it methodically. It felt physically uncomfortable to just sit and wait for everyone else to finish. So, yes, it definitely happened in school, pretty much exactly like what I do now in my sprint planning meetings, just... you know, the seven-year-old version of it. I don't know about movies as much, maybe I get up for popcorn more than most people, but school, absolutely. It was a whole big thing with my teachers.

Have you noticed these kinds of difficulties—like trouble staying seated, feeling restless, or having a hard time staying focused—outside of school and work, such as in social situations, at home, or during other daily activities?

Well, yes, actually. It’s funny you ask about home and other activities because, honestly, it’s not always just about physically getting up and walking away, like I do in those meetings or like I did in Mrs. Gable’s class. Sometimes I *am* sitting down, like if I’m watching a movie with my husband—he loves those really long, slow-burn historical dramas, you know the ones that are like three hours long and take forever to get to the point?—and I’ll be sitting there on the couch, and to him, it probably looks like I’m just relaxing and watching the movie. 

But inside... inside it’s a totally different story. It’s like this intense, buzzing pressure building up in my chest or my arms. Even when I’m sitting calmly on the outside, I feel this overwhelming need to just *move*. I’ll start thinking, "I should be doing something else, I need to switch tasks, I should be folding laundry or checking my email." And if I force myself to just stay still and watch the movie, I have to be doing something with my hands. I’ll pick at my cuticles, or I’ll grab my phone and just scroll through absolutely nothing, or I’ll fiddle with the remote, because if I don’t channel that energy somewhere, I literally feel like I’m going to crawl right out of my skin. 

It happens when I’m sitting in traffic, too, or waiting at the dentist's office. Just this constant, humming restlessness that never really turns off, even when my body is technically staying put. It’s exhausting, honestly, feeling like my brain is revving an engine in neutral all the time.
Have you ever had trouble keeping your attention on tasks or often found yourself easily distracted, even when you wanted to stay focused?

Oh, absolutely. Yes, all the time. It's incredibly frustrating because, like I said, I really do want to focus, especially when it's something important. But it’s like my brain just has a completely different agenda. 

Take work, for example. As a software developer, a huge part of my job is reviewing pull requests from the other engineers on my team. And these aren't simple things, they can be really complex pieces of code where you have to trace the logic and make sure it's not going to break something else in the application. So I’ll sit down at my desk, open up the PR, and I’ll have every intention of just getting through it. I’ll tell myself, "Okay, we are doing this now, focus." And for the first, I don't know, maybe two or three minutes, I'm doing it. I'm reading the code. 

But then, before I even realize it's happening, I'll suddenly become aware that I've been staring at the exact same block of code, the same five lines, for I don't even know how long, and I haven't actually processed a single word of it. Because while my eyes are on the screen, my brain is off thinking about what I need to get at the grocery store, or remembering a conversation I had with my sister three days ago, or wondering if I forgot to switch the laundry, or trying to remember the name of that actor who was in that one movie we watched last month. It’s like five different radio stations are playing in my head all at once. 

And it happens with personal stuff, too, not just work. Like I mentioned those mortgage documents for the refinance? My husband printed them all out for us to read through before signing, and it's a massive stack of paper, all this dense legal jargon. I really wanted to understand what we were agreeing to, you know? It's our house, it's a huge financial commitment. So I sat down at the dining room table with my highlighter, ready to tackle it. And again, same exact thing. I'd read a paragraph, and then suddenly I'm thinking about whether we need to call the plumber about that weird noise the sink is making, or if I should look up new paint colors for the guest room. I have to physically force myself to go back and re-read the same paragraph three or four times just to actually absorb the information. It takes me twice as long to get through anything that requires sustained attention because I'm constantly having to reel my brain back in from wherever it wandered off to. It’s just... it's exhausting, having to fight your own mind just to read a document.
When you think back to your childhood, before age 12, were you noticeably more restless, easily distracted, or had trouble focusing compared to other kids your age?

Yeah, so, kind of like I was mentioning a little bit ago when we were talking about Mrs. Gable's third-grade class... it was definitely, noticeably more than the other kids. I think that's actually why it stands out in my memory so much, because I could see the difference even then. 

The other kids would just sit there, you know? They’d be at their little grouped-together desks, just quietly doing their spelling words or practicing their cursive, and then there was me. I know I already told you about how my teachers were always having to remind me to stay seated, and how they actually had to move my desk right up to the front of the room, but it really was because I was just constantly popping up out of my chair while everyone else was perfectly fine staying put. 

And it was the talking, too. I was always the one getting the "let's give someone else a chance" speech because I was just blurting things out and talking before I was called on. I just couldn't hold the thought in my head long enough to raise my hand and wait. And the rushing—oh my gosh, the rushing. Like I said before, I understood the work, I really did, but I would just tear through those assignments. I’d look around and see all my classmates taking their time, writing their letters so neatly, working methodically, and I was just like, done, boom, what's next? Why are we still sitting here? 

It actually made me feel a little bit like an alien sometimes, honestly, because I didn't understand why they *didn't* feel the intense need to get up and move. I remember looking at my friends and thinking, "How are you all just sitting there so quietly?" My mom used to get these notes sent home—not bad notes, exactly, because I wasn't a mean kid or anything, but every single parent-teacher conference and every report card from kindergarten through at least fifth grade had some variation of, "She's a bright girl, but she needs to learn to stay in her seat, slow down, and wait her turn." So, yes, definitely before age 12, and absolutely way more than my classmates. It was basically my defining personality trait in elementary school.
